title: At a Restaurant
pronunciation_focus_summary: GL and GN sounds — unique Italian sounds found in common food words like aglio (garlic), gnocchi, tagliatelle, and famiglia. GL sounds like 'ly' in million. GN sounds like 'ny' in canyon.

phrases.translation: I would like to reserve a table
phrases.pronunciation_notes: Roll the R in 'vorrei' and 'prenotare'. Stress on the second-to-last syllable of 'tavolo'.
phrases.example_sentence: Vorrei prenotare un tavolo per stasera.

phrases.text: Un tavolo per due, per favore
phrases.phonetic_ipa: un ˈtavolo per ˈdue per faˈvore
phrases.phonetic_approx: oon TAH-voh-loh pair DOO-ay pair fah-VOH-ray
phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Due' is two syllables: DOO-ay. 'Favore' stress on the second syllable.
phrases.example_sentence: Buonasera, un tavolo per due, per favore.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Stress falls on the last syllable of 'menù' (indicated by the accent). Clear, open vowels.
phrases.example_sentence: Potrei avere il menù, per favore?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'gli' in 'consiglia' is the GL sound — tongue presses against the palate, like 'ly' in 'million'.
Both words start with 'pr' — practice the rolled R after P. Clear vowels on every syllable.
phrases.example_sentence: Prendo il primo: gli spaghetti alla carbonara.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Double feature! 'Gli' uses the GL sound (ly). 'Gnocchi' uses the GN sound (ny) plus double CC (k-k). Hold the K sound longer.
phrases.example_sentence: Gli gnocchi alla sorrentina sono buonissimi.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'gli' in 'tagliatelle' is the GL sound. Double 'l' in 'telle' — hold it slightly longer.
phrases.example_sentence: Le tagliatelle al ragù sono il piatto tipico di Bologna.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The GL in 'aglio' is the key sound. 'Olio' also has a 'ly' quality. This pasta dish is great GL practice!
phrases.example_sentence: Spaghetti aglio e olio — semplice ma delizioso.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'g' before 'e' in 'vegetariano' is soft like 'j'. Roll the R. Use -o for male, -a for female.
phrases.example_sentence: Sono vegetariana. Avete piatti senza carne?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'z' in 'delizioso' is voiced (dz sound). Clear vowels throughout — every vowel is pronounced.
phrases.example_sentence: Questo risotto è delizioso! Complimenti allo chef.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Simple and essential. Clear vowels, stress on 'KON' in 'conto'.
Every vowel is clearly pronounced. Stress on 'PA'. The word literally means 'before the meal'.
Double 't' in 'piatto' — hold the T sound longer. This distinguishes it from 'piato' which isn't a word.
phrases.example_sentence: Come secondo piatto, prendo il pesce.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Bottiglia' has both double T and the GL sound. Double S in 'rosso'. Roll the R in 'rosso'.
phrases.example_sentence: Una bottiglia di vino rosso della casa, per favore.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Double P in 'appetito' — hold the P slightly longer. 'Buon' has the 'wo' diphthong.
phrases.example_sentence: Ecco i vostri piatti. Buon appetito!

dialogues.context: Ordering at a traditional Italian restaurant

exchanges.speaker: waiter
exchanges.translation: Good evening! Do you have a reservation?

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Sì, a nome Rossi. Un tavolo per due.
exchanges.translation: Yes, under the name Rossi. A table for two.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: SEE, ah NOH-may ROHS-see. oon TAH-voh-loh pair DOO-ay

exchanges.speaker: waiter
exchanges.text: Prego, da questa parte. Ecco il menù.
exchanges.translation: Please, this way. Here's the menu.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: PRAY-goh, dah KWES-tah PAHR-tay. EK-koh eel may-NOO

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.translation: Thank you. What do you recommend as a first course?

dialogues.notes: Italian meals traditionally have multiple courses: antipasto (starter), primo (first course — pasta or soup), secondo (main — meat or fish), contorno (side dish), and dolce (dessert). You don't have to order all courses.

cultural_notes.title: The Italian meal structure
cultural_notes.content: Italian dining follows a sacred structure: antipasto (appetizer), primo (first course — always pasta, risotto, or soup), secondo (second course — meat or fish, served alone), contorno (side vegetables, ordered separately), and dolce (dessert). Italians rarely eat pasta as a side dish to meat — that's a foreign invention. The 'coperto' (cover charge) on your bill is normal and legal. Tipping isn't expected but rounding up is kind. Never ask for parmesan on seafood pasta — it's a serious faux pas.
